query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the identity of X governs whether a stable, adherent protective oxide forms during high‐temperature exposure: when X is Al or Si, the alloy preferentially forms slow-growing, coherent oxide scales (predominantly Al2O3 or SiO2) that effectively barrier oxygen and ion diffusion; whereas when X is Mn, rapid outward diffusion leads to the formation of Mn‐rich, non‐coherent oxides that crack and spall. This behavior is further modulated by diffusion-controlled kinetics (i.e., sluggish diffusion due to multicomponent mixing).
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys prepared as single-phase (or controlled multiphase) metallic solid solutions with X = Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Systematically substituting X to compare alloys with Al or Si versus Mn while keeping the base CrFeCoNi components constant.
generation.conditions: Exposure in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C for an extended period.
generation.structural_mediator: The composition, continuity, and adhesion of the surface oxide layer – whether it is a dense, coherent Al2O3/SiO2 layer versus a porous, cracked Mn-rich oxide layer.
generation.mechanism: Protective behavior is governed by differing thermodynamic stabilities and kinetic diffusion rates: Al and Si form oxides with lower free energy that grow slowly and remain coherent, effectively barring oxygen ingress, while Mn, with its higher diffusivity and lower stability in forming coherent oxides, leads to rapid oxide growth that is prone to cracking and spallation. These differences modulate the outward cation diffusion versus inward oxygen diffusion dynamics, further controlled by diffusion-controlled kinetics inherent to the high-entropy alloy matrix.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with X = Al or Si are expected to develop thin, adherent, and continuous protective oxide layers that persist during high-temperature exposure, whereas alloys with X = Mn will form thicker, less coherent oxide scales that eventually crack and spall, compromising protection.
generation.baseline: A defined baseline is provided by the CrFeCoNiMn alloy, which under identical exposure conditions displays non-protective, unstable Mn-rich oxide formation. Comparisons between this and the Al- or Si-containing alloys serve to highlight the role of the X component.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies for alloys in a metallic solid-solution state (whether single- or controlled multiphase) when exposed to oxidative or corrosive atmospheres at temperatures exceeding 900 °C; effects may vary outside these conditions or with different microstructural states.
generation.uncertainty: While the proposed mechanism is backed by thermodynamic and kinetic considerations, uncertainties remain regarding the influence of minor phase segregation, grain boundary character, and long-term elemental depletion effects that may modify oxide adhesion over extended exposures.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloy samples with X = Si, Mn, and Al in identical single-phase (or comparable multiphase) states. Subject all samples to identical high-temperature oxidation tests (e.g., 925–1000 °C in air for 50 hours). Characterize the oxide scale formation using SEM, EDS, XRD, and adhesion tests.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness and uniformity (via cross-sectional microscopy)
Adhesion and spallation behavior (through mechanical tests)
Elemental diffusion profiles near the oxide/substrate interface (via EDS mapping)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al- or Si-containing alloys do not form a thinner, continuous, and adherent oxide layer (i.e. if they form oxide scales similar in morphology, thickness, and tendency to crack/spall as the Mn-containing alloy), or if the Mn-containing alloy unexpectedly develops a stable, protective oxide comparable to that of the Al/Si alloys, then the hypothesis is falsified.

However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
